study_identification.author_journal_year: Jalbrzikowski et al., American Journal of Psychiatry, 2019
study_identification.title: Age-Associated Deviations of Amygdala Functional Connectivity in Youths With Psychosis Spectrum Disorders: Relevance to Psychotic Symptoms

study_characteristics.study_objective: To create normative growth charts of amygdala functional connectivity in typically developing youths, assess age-associated deviations of these trajectories in youths with psychosis spectrum disorders, and explore how these disruptions are related to clinical symptomatology.
study_characteristics.study_design_other: Three cross-sectional and one longitudinal dataset were combined. The control group included longitudinal data, while the psychosis spectrum group only included cross-sectional data.

dataset_name.answer: Luna 1 (University of Pittsburgh); Luna 2 (University of Pittsburgh); Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC); Neurodevelopmental Cohort Pitt

hc_age.answer: Luna 1: mean 16.7, sd 3.0, range 10-25; Luna 2: mean 19.5, sd 3.6, range 14-25; PNC: mean 16.2, sd 3.4, range 10-22; Pitt: mean 21.0, sd 2.7, range 12-25

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: AFNI 3dDeconvolve; AFNI 3dREML; Wavelet Despiking; ICA-AROMA for motion artifact removal; FreeSurfer automated segmentation; spatial smoothing (5mm FWHM Gaussian kernel); bandpass filtering (0.009 Hz < f < 0.08); nuisance regression (NBT, white matter, ventricular signal, 6 head realignment parameters and their derivatives)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Frame displacement (FD) and DVARS calculated for head motion; volumes with FD > 0.3 mm and/or DVARS > 20 were censored and removed; subjects dropped if more than 20% of volumes were removed; sensitivity analyses conducted by removing high-motion subjects (top 25%, >0.17 mm average FD); motion covariates included in all analyses

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Site included as fixed effect in linear mixed-effects models (3dLME in AFNI). Site differences were effectively removed by including site as a covariate, verified by residual analysis showing no significant differences between sites after adjustment (all χ²=0, p=1). Age-associated changes were remarkably consistent across different samples.

response_variable.answer: Resting-state functional connectivity between amygdala subregions (centromedial and basolateral) and whole brain voxels

predictor_effects.answer: Age, sex, and site were modeled as fixed effects. Subject was included as a random effect to account for nonindependence of data in the longitudinal cohort.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study appropriately handled multiple nuisance structures including: 1) Site effects modeled as fixed effects in linear mixed-effects models; 2) Motion artifacts addressed through multiple approaches (ICA-AROMA, wavelet despiking, volume censoring based on FD and DVARS); 3) Head motion included as covariate (average framewise displacement); 4) Subject-level random effects to account for non-independence in longitudinal data; 5) Extensive validation including sensitivity analyses excluding high-motion subjects and confirming results remain significant when motion covariates added; 6) Residual analyses verifying adequate site adjustment; 7) Multiple forms of age tested (linear, inverse, quadratic) with model selection based on AIC/BIC.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Site, sex, and framewise displacement were included as fixed effects. Subject was included as a random effect, which allows us to model and account for the nonindependence of data (multiple visits) in the longitudinal cohort... To ensure that motion artifacts did not drive our results, we extracted the mean region of interest from the significant clusters and reran the linear mixed-effects models, including average framewise displacement as an additional fixed effect. We also reran developmental analyses on subsets of 'low-motion' subjects, removing participants with average framewise displacement in the upper 25th percentile (framewise displacement > 0.17 mm)... We also confirmed that site effects were appropriately accounted for by including the measure as a covariate. After regressing out the effects of site in each region, we then plotted the residuals. The residuals all clustered around zero, which provides evidence that we were able to effectively account for site in our model. Furthermore, when we conducted a mixed-model linear regression to compare residuals between sites, there were no significant differences between sites for any of the regions of interest (all x² = 0, p = 1).
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Main text p.199 lines 46-70; p.202 lines 122-125; Supplement Table S3-S4

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study validated the normative model using the same training dataset through multiple approaches: 1) Model fit assessed using multiple comparisons correction (cluster-wise p<0.05 with Monte Carlo simulation); 2) Sensitivity analyses excluding high-motion subjects showed all significant age effects remained; 3) Motion covariates added and results remained significant; 4) Multiple forms of age tested with model selection (inverse form showed best fit based on AIC/BIC); 5) Residual analyses confirmed adequate modeling of site effects.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: For clusters for which significant results were obtained across multiple forms of age (linear, inverse, quadratic), we determined a conjunction cluster and extracted the cluster's mean region of interest for each individual. We reran the mixed-effects models described above with linear, inverse, and quadratic forms of age on these data. The model with the lowest combination of the Akaike information criterion and the Bayesian information criterion was considered to be the best fitting one... All developmental effects remained significant when motion covariates (average framewise displacement) and MRI software version were included in the model and when high-motion subjects were excluded from the analysis.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Main text p.199 lines 66-70; p.202 lines 119-122

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study did not employ independent hold-out validation within the same domain (i.e., splitting the typically developing control group into training and test sets). All 622 typically developing controls were used to build the normative model without independent validation on a separate subset of controls.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: No explicit mention of independent validation using held-out controls from the same datasets. The entire control sample (N=622) was used for model development.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.location: Main text p.197 Table 1; Methods section does not describe train/test splitting

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study did not validate the normative model on an independent external dataset from a different domain or collection. All four datasets (Luna 1, Luna 2, PNC, Pitt) were combined into a single normative model without external validation on completely independent cohorts.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: No mention of external validation on independent datasets not included in the model development. The study combined data from four samples but did not reserve any external dataset for validation.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Methods section does not describe external validation

clinical_dataset.answer: Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort (PNC); Neurodevelopmental Cohort Pitt

diseases_studied.answer: Psychosis Spectrum Disorders; Other Psychopathology (non-psychotic psychiatric disorders meeting DSM-IV criteria)

clinical_groups_age.answer: Psychosis spectrum: PNC mean 16.0, sd 2.9; Pitt mean 20.8, sd 3.1; Other psychopathology: PNC mean 16.4, sd 3.3

clinical_groups_sex.answer: Psychosis spectrum: F 162 (83.5%), M 87 (44.8%); Other psychopathology: F 246 (100%), M 150 (61.0%)

deviation_metric.answer: Brain maturation deviation score: absolute value of the difference between individual's actual connectivity and predicted normative connectivity based on age-matched expected value from the typically developing model

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Linear mixed-effects models with inverse age-by-group interaction terms to assess age-associated deviations. False discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons (q < 0.1). Slope comparison analyses using least-squares means (lsmeans). Pearson correlations between brain maturation deviation scores and positive symptoms. Post hoc analyses examined direction of relationships during specific developmental periods with significant group differences, controlling for age, sex, and motion.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Youths with psychosis spectrum disorders failed to show typical age-associated decreases in centromedial amygdala connectivity with striatum, thalamus, lateral prefrontal cortex, and occipital cortex, with greater age-related deviation in amygdala-thalamus connectivity associated with increased positive symptoms.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: In typically developing youths, significant age-related decreases were observed in centromedial amygdala connectivity with 19 brain regions including bilateral posterior cingulate, insula, parahippocampal cortex, precentral gyrus/frontal eye fields, left ventrolateral and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, left caudate and putamen, right thalamus, and right occipital cortex (all FDR corrected). In contrast, youths with psychosis spectrum disorders failed to exhibit significant age-associated changes in connectivity between centromedial amygdala and six regions: left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (χ²=7.5, p=0.006, q=0.04), left putamen (χ²=8.2, p=0.004, q=0.04), right thalamus (χ²=6.7, p=0.009, q=0.05), left caudate (χ²=8.5, p=0.004, q=0.04), left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (χ²=4.1, p=0.04, q=0.09), and right middle occipital cortex (χ²=5.4, p=0.02, q=0.05). During late childhood (ages 10-14), the psychosis spectrum group exhibited significantly lower connectivity compared to controls in these regions, but in adulthood (ages 17-25.9), they exhibited higher connectivity, reflecting a lack of normative developmental decreases. Age-associated alterations in centromedial amygdala-putamen and amygdala-occipital connectivity were unique to the psychosis spectrum group and not observed in the other psychopathology group. Greater age-related deviation in centromedial amygdala-thalamus connectivity was significantly associated with increased severity of positive symptoms in the psychosis spectrum group (r=0.19, p=0.01, q=0.05), specifically grandiose ideas (r=0.31, p<0.001) and hallucinations (r=0.23, p=0.003), but not unusual thought content. During late childhood/early adolescence, lower amygdala-thalamus connectivity was associated with greater positive symptoms (r=-0.27, p=0.01, q=0.05). This relationship was not present for negative, depressive, or manic symptoms, nor in the other psychopathology group.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Cross-sectional data for psychosis spectrum group prevents definitive conclusions about altered development versus abnormalities due to time of psychosis onset; cannot demonstrate within-person change; longitudinal studies with multiple visits per individual needed to identify how subject-specific trajectories diverge/converge from typical development; psychotic symptoms are dynamic and change over time, requiring time-varying analytic approaches; statistically significant site effects observed in many regions despite all scans on same scanner model due to differences in task instructions, MRI resolution, and scan duration; site effects may have obscured smaller developmental changes and more subtle age-related deviations; harmonization methods (e.g., from genetics) should be applied to resting-state connectivity data in future work; small effect size for symptom-connectivity relationship (r=0.19) requires replication.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study represents a proof-of-principle approach for merging multiple resting-state fMRI datasets to inform normative developmental trajectories. Despite samples having multiple sites, protocols, and recruitment methods, age-associated changes were remarkably consistent across samples. The growth charting method establishes a novel connection between deviations from amygdala-thalamus connectivity development and positive symptom severity. Results highlight the importance of examining role of (dys)maturation patterns in psychiatric disorder development and suggest multisite neuroimaging datasets will be important for understanding how biomarkers may be sensitive or specific to developmental stage.

general_notes.general_notes: This study uses a growth chart approach, typically used for metrics like weight and head circumference, extended to assess psychiatric disorders' relationship to deviations from normative brain development. The study combined data from four samples: three from University of Pittsburgh (Luna 1, Luna 2, Pitt) and one from University of Pennsylvania (PNC). All scans were acquired on Siemens 3T Tim Trio scanners but with different protocols (see Supplementary Table S2 for detailed parameters). The centromedial and basolateral amygdala subregions were defined using FSL's Juelich histological atlas with voxels having at least 50% probability. Multiple comparisons correction used Monte Carlo simulation (3dClustSim) requiring 30 contiguous voxels with single voxel threshold p<0.001 for cluster-wise corrected p<0.05. The inverse form of age provided the best fit for all significant clusters based on AIC and BIC. Sex-specific HC demographics from Table 1: Luna 1 (F 100, M 113), Luna 2 (F 43, M 45), PNC (F 141, M 151), Pitt (F 11, M 18). Clinical groups came only from PNC (psychosis spectrum: 162; other psychopathology: 246) and Pitt (psychosis spectrum: 32). Psychiatric medication status was included as covariate and all significant age-by-group interactions remained. No significant interactions observed for inverse age × group × sex, inverse age × group × site, sex × group, or group × site.
